quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on welts, stitching ends, wadding picks and the loose-back, fast-back and waved forms of piqué.

questions.q: In which direction do the cords of a plain welt piqué run?
options: Warp-way, along the cloth
Diagonally
Weft-way, across the cloth
They form a check in both directions
questions.explain: The stitching picks run across the cloth, so the furrows and the cords between them are weft-way. Warp-way cords are the Bedford cord of the previous lecture.

questions.q: What is the role of the stitching warp in a piqué?
options: Held at high tension, it is lifted over the face on the stitching picks and pulls the face down into a furrow
It weaves plain with the face picks to form the cord surface
It lies straight inside the cord as wadding
It is a coloured warp that gives the cord its colour
questions.explain: The stitching (back) ends are tight and are raised only on the stitching picks; their pull on the slack face cloth makes the indent. Wadding is a weft, not a warp.

questions.q: What is the usual proportion of stitching ends to face ends?
options: One stitching end for every face end
One stitching end for every two face ends
Two stitching ends for every face end
One stitching end for every six face ends
questions.explain: The lecture gives one stitching end for every two face ends; in the 6-end welt, ends 2 and 5 are the stitching ends among four face ends.

questions.q: What are wadding picks?
options: Fine picks that weave plain on the back
Picks that interlace only with the stitching ends
The two picks on which the stitching ends are lifted
Thick picks laid between face and back to fill the cords
questions.explain: Wadding picks are coarse weft laid under the face and over the stitching ends so that the cords are padded out; they do not form the indent.

questions.q: In a piqué the face warp and the stitching warp are held at the same tension.
questions.explain: The stitching warp is held at high tension and the face warp is comparatively slack; the difference is what lets the tight back ends pull the face into furrows.

questions.q: What distinguishes a fast-back welt from a loose-back welt?
options: The fast-back has no wadding picks
The fast-back uses a twill face
In the fast-back the stitching ends also interlace with the wadding picks, locking the back
The fast-back has stitching ends on every pick
questions.explain: In the loose-back version the wadding simply lies over the stitching ends; in the fast-back the stitching ends interlace with the wadding too, so the back is bound firm.

questions.q: How is a waved piqué produced?
options: The stitching points move diagonally from pick to pick so the furrow waves
The wadding picks are inserted in a wavy order
The face warp is coloured in waves
The cloth is embossed after weaving
questions.explain: Shifting the stitching points diagonally across the repeat makes the furrow run in a wave instead of a straight line across the cloth; the lecture shows a 24 × 24 and a 30 × 16 example.

questions.q: Wadding picks appear on the face of the cloth between the cords.
questions.explain: They lie under the face and over the stitching ends, hidden inside the cord; the face shows only the plain-weaving face warp and face picks.

questions.q: Why does the lecture call piqué "two warps, one cloth"?
options: Because two separate cloths are woven and stitched together
Because a face warp and a stitching warp are woven with one set of weft into a single cloth
Because the face warp is doubled
Because the weft is used in two colours
questions.explain: A piqué has two warps (face and stitching) but one weft system, and the result is one cloth, not a double cloth with two separate layers.

questions.q: The furrow, or indent, forms where the stitching ends are lifted over the face.
questions.explain: On the stitching picks the tight back ends are raised over the face and pull it down; between those lines the face bulges into a cord.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How the welt repeat, the heald count and the cord shape respond to stitching picks, wadding and tension.

questions.q: In the 6-pick welt of the lecture, how are the picks divided?
options: 3 face picks and 3 stitching picks
6 face picks, with the stitching ends lifted on every pick
4 face picks and 2 stitching picks (picks 5–6)
2 face picks and 4 wadding picks
questions.explain: The stitching ends are down on all face picks and lifted on picks 5–6, which the lecture calls the indent; four face picks weave plain in between.

questions.q: Adding wadding picks 3–4 to the welt changes its repeat from 6 ends × 6 picks to what?
options: 8 ends × 6 picks
6 ends × 8 picks
6 ends × 6 picks (unchanged)
12 ends × 12 picks
questions.explain: Two extra picks are added, so the repeat becomes 6 ends × 8 picks. The number of ends is not affected by extra picks.

questions.q: A piqué has 24 face ends in a repeat and one stitching end for every two face ends. How many stitching ends are in the repeat?
questions.explain: 24 face ends ÷ 2 = 12 stitching ends, giving 36 ends in all.

questions.q: If the tension on the stitching warp is increased, what happens to the cloth?
options: The cords become flatter
The wadding picks move to the face
The face warp becomes tighter too
The furrows become deeper and the cords more pronounced
questions.explain: The indent is made by the tight stitching ends pulling the face down; more tension gives a deeper furrow and a bolder cord.

questions.q: Using a thicker yarn for the wadding picks will make the cords:
options: Fuller and rounder
Narrower
Flatter
Less visible on the face
questions.explain: Wadding fills the space between face and back; a thicker wadding pads the cord out more, so it stands fuller and rounder.

questions.q: A waved piqué needs a larger repeat than a straight welt.
questions.explain: The straight welt repeats on 6 ends × 6 picks, but moving the stitching points diagonally needs 24 × 24 or 30 × 16 in the lecture's examples before the pattern returns to its start.

questions.q: The wadding pick is written as $B4. What is this in binary (8 bits)?
questions.explain: $B = 1011 and $4 = 0100, so $B4 = 1011 0100; the first six bits give the six ends, the last two are padding.

questions.q: What makes the face bulge up into a cord between two furrows?
options: The wadding picks pushing the stitching ends down
The face picks being tighter than the stitching picks
The slack face cloth is pulled down only at the stitching lines, so it rises between them
The face warp is lifted over the stitching ends
questions.explain: The face warp is slack and is pulled down only where the tight stitching ends cross it, so between those lines it stands up as a cord; wadding merely fills the space.

questions.q: The welt is drafted 1 2 3 1 2 3 on 3 healds. How many ends are on heald 2?
questions.explain: Each heald carries 6 ÷ 3 = 2 ends; heald 2 carries ends 2 and 5, the two stitching ends.

questions.q: Which ends are down on every face pick of the welt?
options: The stitching ends
The face ends on heald 1
The face ends on heald 3
Every end on alternate picks
questions.explain: The stitching ends stay down on all face picks and lift only on the stitching picks; the face ends alternate up and down as plain weave.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting ends, picks, cords and hex digits from the welt and waved piqué drafts.

questions.q: The wadding pick $B4 covers 6 ends (the first 6 bits of 1011 0100). How many ends are lifted on this pick?
questions.explain: Bits 1 0 1 1 0 1 contain four 1s: ends 1, 3, 4 and 6 (the face ends) are lifted; ends 2 and 5 (stitching) stay down.

questions.q: A face warp has 1,200 ends. With one stitching end for every two face ends, how many stitching ends are needed?
questions.explain: 1,200 ÷ 2 = 600 stitching ends on the back beam.

questions.q: A piqué warp has 1,800 ends in total, made up of face and stitching ends in the ratio 2 : 1. How many are stitching ends?
questions.explain: Face : stitching = 2 : 1, so stitching ends are one third of the total: 1,800 ÷ 3 = 600 (and 1,200 face ends).

questions.q: A plain welt repeats on 6 picks and the cloth is woven at 60 picks per inch. How many cords are there per inch?
questions.explain: Each 6-pick repeat makes one cord and one furrow, so 60 ÷ 6 = 10 cords per inch.

questions.q: The loose-back welt with wadding repeats on 8 picks. At 72 picks per inch, how many repeats are there per inch?
questions.explain: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 repeats (cords) per inch.

questions.q: The second waved piqué repeats on 30 ends. At 90 ends per inch, what is the width of one repeat in inches (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: 30 ÷ 90 = 0.333 inch, so three repeats fit in each inch of width.

questions.q: A pick on 6 ends lifts ends 1, 4 and 6 only. With two padding zeros, what is its hex code?
questions.explain: Ends 1–6 give 1 0 0 1 0 1, plus 00 padding: 1001 0100 = $94. $A4 would lift ends 1, 3 and 6; $92 would lift ends 1, 4 and 7.

questions.q: In the 8-pick loose-back welt, picks 3–4 are wadding. What percentage of the picks are wadding picks?
questions.explain: 2 wadding picks out of 8 = 25 %.

questions.q: In the 6-end welt drafted 1 2 3 1 2 3, which healds carry the face ends?
options: Healds 1 and 2
Heald 2 only
Healds 1 and 3
All three healds
questions.explain: Ends 1 and 4 are on heald 1, ends 3 and 6 on heald 3 — these four are the face ends. Heald 2 carries the two stitching ends.

questions.q: The wadding pick $B4 lifts ends 1, 3, 4 and 6.
questions.explain: 1011 01 read across ends 1–6 gives lifts on ends 1, 3, 4 and 6, i.e. all the face ends, so the wadding passes under the face and over the stitching ends 2 and 5.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Sampling, loom and costing decisions for welts and piqués in a weaving shed.

questions.q: A welt sample shows almost no furrow and the cords are flat. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too many face ends
The stitching warp was woven at too low a tension
The wadding picks were too thick
The face weave was 2/2 twill instead of plain
questions.explain: The indent is made by tight stitching ends pulling the face down; if they are slack the pull is weak and the furrow disappears. Thick wadding would make cords rounder, not flatter.

questions.q: A buyer wants heavier, rounder cords in the same welt design. What is the usual answer?
options: Double the number of stitching ends
Change to a fast-back construction
Reduce the picks per inch
Add thick wadding picks between the face and the stitching ends
questions.explain: Wadding picks fill the cords and add weight. More stitching ends would only add more pull points, and fewer picks make a lighter cloth.

questions.q: In a loose-back welt with wadding, the loose wadding on the back snags during making-up. Which construction solves this?
options: Fast-back welt, where the stitching ends interlace with the wadding picks
Waved piqué
A welt without stitching ends
A welt with wadding on the face
questions.explain: The fast-back locks the wadding in place by interlacing it with the stitching ends, so nothing lies loose on the back.

questions.q: Why does a piqué normally need two warp beams?
options: Because the face warp is wider than the back warp
Because the two warps are different colours
Because the stitching warp is held at high tension and the face warp slack, and they take up at different rates
Because the wadding has to be wound on its own beam
questions.explain: Different tensions and different take-up cannot be managed from one beam; wadding is weft, so it needs no beam at all.

questions.q: Wadding picks can be a coarse, cheap yarn because they are hidden inside the cord.
questions.explain: The wadding lies under the face and over the stitching ends and is never seen, so bulk per rupee matters more than appearance or strength.

questions.q: Why would the 24-end × 24-pick waved piqué be woven on a dobby rather than a tappet loom?
options: Because it needs more than two warp beams
Because the lifting order changes over a 24-pick repeat, beyond what tappets conveniently give
Because wadding picks cannot be inserted on a tappet loom
Because the face weave is not plain
questions.explain: Tappets suit short, fixed repeats; a 24-pick repeat with diagonally moving stitching points needs the programmable lifting of a dobby.

questions.q: The weaver reports frequent breaks in the stitching ends. What is the likely reason and the sensible first step?
options: The stitching ends are too slack; raise the tension
The face ends are too coarse; use a finer face count
They are the most highly tensioned ends in the cloth; use a stronger yarn or ease the tension slightly
The wadding picks are cutting them; remove the wadding
questions.explain: The stitching warp carries the highest tension, so it breaks first; a stronger yarn (or a modest tension reduction that still gives a furrow) is the normal cure.

questions.q: A welt can be woven satisfactorily from a single warp beam provided the face and stitching ends are the same count.
questions.explain: Count is not the issue: the two warps need different tensions and take up at different rates, so they must be controlled separately.

questions.q: A finer yarn is substituted for the wadding picks to save cost. What will the customer notice?
options: Deeper furrows
More stitching lines
A rougher face
Flatter, less rounded cords
questions.explain: Wadding gives the cords their fullness, so finer wadding means less padding and flatter cords; the furrows and face are unchanged.

questions.q: Which statement about loose-back and fast-back welts is correct?
options: The fast-back has a more stable back because its stitching ends interlace with the wadding
The loose-back has no wadding picks at all
The fast-back is woven without a stitching warp
The loose-back always has deeper furrows
questions.explain: The only structural difference is that in the fast-back the stitching ends also bind the wadding picks, which makes the back firmer; both can carry wadding.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that link piqué to Bedford cord, read hex codes and reason in two steps about cord formation.

questions.q: What is the essential structural difference between a Bedford cord and a welt piqué?
options: Bedford cord uses wadding; piqué never does
Bedford cord is a twill; piqué is plain
Bedford cord makes warp-way cords with back weft floats; piqué makes weft-way cords with a tight stitching warp
There is none; the two names describe the same cloth
questions.explain: A Bedford cord raises warp-way ribs by weft floats on the back; a piqué pulls the face into weft-way furrows with a tight back warp. Both may use filling yarns (stuffer ends or wadding picks).

questions.q: A piqué has 72 face ends per inch and one stitching end for every two face ends. What is the total ends per inch?
questions.explain: Stitching ends = 72 ÷ 2 = 36; total = 72 + 36 = 108 ends per inch.

questions.q: On the stitching picks (5–6) of the welt, what happens to the face warp?
options: All the face ends are lifted so the picks lie on the back
The face ends continue to interlace with the weft while the stitching ends are lifted over the face
The face ends are all lowered
The face ends are replaced by wadding
questions.explain: The stitching picks are still woven into the face; what changes is that the stitching ends come up over the face on those picks and pull it into the furrow.

questions.q: In the loose-back welt the wadding picks interlace with no ends at all; they are held only by lying between the face and the stitching ends.
questions.explain: On the wadding pick all face ends are up and all stitching ends down, so the pick passes between the two layers without crossing any end; only the fast-back binds it.

questions.q: A student codes the wadding pick as $4B instead of $B4. What would the loom do?
options: Exactly the same as $B4, since hex is read either way
Lift the stitching ends and lower the face ends, so the wadding would lie on the face
Lift every end
Lower every end
questions.explain: $4B = 0100 1011: ends 2 and 5 (stitching) up, face ends 1, 3, 4 down — the mirror of the intended lift, putting the thick pick on the face instead of under it.

questions.q: The plain welt repeats on 6 × 6 squares and the waved piqué on 24 × 24. How many times larger in area is the waved repeat?
questions.explain: 576 ÷ 36 = 16: the waved design needs sixteen times the point-paper area before it returns to its start.

questions.q: Why do the stitching ends stay almost invisible on the face in a well-made welt?
options: They are finer than the face ends
They are the same colour as the wadding
They are lifted only on two picks of six and lie down under the face on all the others
They are cut away in finishing
questions.explain: Being down on all the face picks and up only on the stitching picks, they show only along the furrow, where the face is pulled down over them.

questions.q: A mill raises the stitching warp tension and at the same time adds thick wadding picks. What combined effect should it expect?
options: Deeper furrows and rounder, heavier cords
Flatter cords and shallower furrows
No change, because the two effects cancel
Cords that move from weft-way to warp-way
questions.explain: Tension deepens the indent; wadding fills the cord. The two act on different parts of the structure and reinforce the relief.

questions.q: Wadding picks increase the cloth weight and the fullness of the cords without showing on the face.
questions.explain: They lie hidden under the face, so they add weight and bulk but no visible change to the face appearance.

questions.q: A customer wants exactly 10 cords per inch. Which construction and pick density gives that?
options: A 6-pick welt woven at 60 picks per inch
An 8-pick loose-back welt at 64 picks per inch
A 6-pick welt at 64 picks per inch
An 8-pick loose-back welt at 72 picks per inch
questions.explain: Cords per inch = picks per inch ÷ picks per repeat: 60 ÷ 6 = 10. The others give 8, 10.7 and 9 cords per inch.
